title: Word Search

problem.description:
Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word exists in the grid.

The word can be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. The same letter cell may not be used more than once.

Example 1:

Input: board = [["A","B","C","E"],["S","F","C","S"],["A","D","E","E"]], word = "ABCCED"
Output: true

Example 2:

Input: board = [["A","B","C","E"],["S","F","C","S"],["A","D","E","E"]], word = "SEE"
Output: true

Example 3:

Input: board = [["A","B","C","E"],["S","F","C","S"],["A","D","E","E"]], word = "ABCB"
Output: false

Constraints:

- m == board.length

- n = board[i].length

- 1 <= m, n <= 6

- 1 <= word.length <= 15

- board and word consists of only lowercase and uppercase English letters.

Follow up: Could you use search pruning to make your solution faster with a larger board?

hints: You need to decide whether you can trace the word letter by letter through the grid, stepping only up, down, left or right each time, and never stepping on the same cell twice in one trace.

Look at Example 3: the path A, B, C exists and a B sits right next to that C, but it is the B you already used. So you must remember which cells the current path has visited, and this choice depends on the path, not just on the cell.

The board has at most 36 cells and the word at most 15 letters. After the first letter, each step has at most 3 new directions, so roughly `36 * 3^14` paths is a loose worst-case bound that real pruning cuts down sharply. An exponential search is acceptable here because the inputs are tiny and there is no polynomial trick.
This is backtracking, which is a depth-first search over grid paths. It fits because you extend a partial path one cell at a time, and you undo your choice when that path cannot be completed.
Abandon a path the moment the current cell does not match the next needed letter. Mark the cell as used while you explore from it, then unmark it when you return, so other paths can still use it.

Track your current cell `(r, c)` and an index `k` meaning `word[0..k-1]` has already been matched along this path. Also keep a visited marker, for example by temporarily overwriting `board[r][c]` with a sentinel character and restoring it afterwards.

Try every cell in the grid as a possible start with `k = 0`.
At a cell: if it is out of bounds, already used, or not equal to `word[k]`, fail.
If `k` is the last index of the word, succeed.
Mark the cell as used.
Recurse into the 4 neighbors with `k + 1`, and stop as soon as one succeeds.
Unmark the cell and return the result.
Return true if any start succeeds, otherwise false.

The trickiest step is restoring the cell on every exit path, including early returns, or later searches will break. Handle a one-letter word and a word longer than `m * n`. Useful pruning: return false immediately if the board lacks enough copies of some letter the word needs. Also reverse the word when its last letter is rarer on the board than its first, so the search starts from fewer cells. Time is `O(m * n * 3^L)` and extra space is `O(L)` for the recursion depth.

normal.note: Path that zigzags across the middle row and up to the top row.
Path that walks around a 2x2 square.
Needs backtracking over several A cells before finding the B.
Lowercase letters, path starting from a non-corner start.

edge.note: Single cell: the one-letter word matches.
Cell reuse: the single cell cannot be used twice.
Single row: the path goes from right to left.
Case sensitivity: uppercase A does not match lowercase a.
All-equal letters: the word is longer than the number of cells.
Tricky backtracking: the long path loops through the E cluster.

review.summary: Your backtracking plan is right, but the visited check is inverted and two directions recurse into the wrong cell, so every word longer than one letter returns false.
review.yourIdea: You start a DFS from every cell that matches `word[0]`. From each cell you try the four neighbours that match the next letter, mark the current cell as used while you go deeper, and unmark it when you backtrack. You stop with true once `k` reaches the word length.

gaps.title: What the visited array means got flipped
gaps.explanation: `vis[x][y] == true` means the cell is already on your current path, so it must NOT be reused. Your guards only allow stepping onto cells where `vis` is true, which is the opposite. `vis` starts all false, and you only set it when a move succeeds, so the very first call can never move anywhere. To keep the invariant straight, say it in words ("I can step onto a neighbour if it is in bounds, unused, and matches the next letter") and check that each condition matches that sentence.

bugs.issue: The neighbour is allowed only if it is already visited (`vis[...]` instead of `!vis[...]`).
The Left branch checks `(r, c-1)` but recurses into `(r, c+1)`. Once the vis check is fixed, this can step outside the grid, and `vis[r][c] = true` on the next level then writes out of bounds.
bugs.fix: Recurse with `solve(board, word, r, c-1, k+1, vis)`.

bugs.issue: The Up branch checks `(r-1, c)` but recurses into `(r+1, c)`, which is the same copy-paste slip.
bugs.fix: Recurse with `solve(board, word, r-1, c, k+1, vis)`.

bugs.issue: `word` is passed by value, so every recursive call copies the string. That adds up to a factor of about 15 in work.

counterexample.why: `solve(0,0,k=1)` checks Right: `(0,1)` is in bounds and matches 'B', but `vis[0][1]` is false, so the guard on line 22 fails. No other direction is in bounds, so it returns false.

complexity.time: O(m·n·4·3^(L-1)), times an extra factor of L because the string is copied on each call
complexity.space: O(m·n) for vis plus O(L) recursion depth (O(L^2) with the string copies)
complexity.verdict: Once fixed, the worst case is about 36·4·3^14 ≈ 7×10^8 steps, but pruning on mismatched letters makes real runs far smaller, so it fits easily, especially if you pass `word` by reference.

review.nudge: Read line 15 out loud: "I may step down if the cell below is visited..." Is that the rule you meant? After that, compare each branch's `check(...)` coordinates with the coordinates you pass to `solve(...)` in the same branch.
review.correctIdea: Use DFS with backtracking. From each cell matching `word[0]`, recurse into the in-bounds, unvisited neighbours that match the next character. Mark a cell before exploring from it and unmark it afterwards, so other paths can use it again. For pruning, first make sure the board has enough of each letter in the word. If the last letter of the word is rarer on the board than the first, search for the reversed word instead, which cuts down the number of starting points.
strengths: Correct overall backtracking structure, with mark, recurse, unmark, and an early return on success
The bounds helper `check` is clean and is evaluated before indexing, thanks to short-circuiting
The base case `k == word.length()` correctly handles single-letter words
